title: Big Ben’s clock is kept on time with a stack of old pennies

cover.alt: The Elizabeth Tower at the Palace of Westminster in London, with a dial of the Great Clock near the top, against a blue sky.

body: The Great Clock in London’s Elizabeth Tower, the one whose bell is Big Ben, is regulated with a small stack of pre-decimal pennies on its pendulum. Adding a coin lifts the pendulum’s centre of mass by a hair, which shortens its effective length and makes it swing very slightly faster: **one penny changes the clock’s rate by 0.4 seconds a day**. The clockmakers add or remove coins to keep it within a few seconds a week. In 2009 three of the pennies were replaced by a £5 commemorative coin.

slides.prompt: Adding a penny to the pendulum makes the clock run faster, not slower. Why?
slides.answer: It lifts the centre of mass
slides.detail: A pendulum’s period depends on its length. A coin on the tray minutely raises the swinging mass’s centre, shortening the effective pendulum, so it swings faster.

slides.label: a day: the change in the clock’s rate from one penny
slides.text: Add a coin and the clock gains, remove one and it loses. In August 2015 it was found running seven seconds fast and corrected by taking coins off.

slides.heading: How a penny speeds the clock

steps.label: A penny is laid on the pendulum
Its centre of mass rises a fraction
Each swing takes slightly less time
The clock gains 0.4 s a day

slides.heading: How accurate is it?
slides.text: The clock keeps time to within a few seconds a week, and the design brief was that the first stroke of each hour be correct to a second against Greenwich Mean Time. On New Year’s Eve 2024 it struck midnight within about five thousandths of a second.

events.text: The clock is installed in the tower
The bell cracks; it still rings today
Three pennies swapped for a £5 coin

slides.question: The clock is running a little fast. What do the clockmakers do?
options: Take a penny off the pendulum
Add a penny to the pendulum
slides.explanation: Removing a coin lowers the centre of mass, lengthening the effective pendulum, so it swings slower and the clock loses about 0.4 s a day per penny.
